summary: Introduces a generic, domain-independent and supplier-independent architecture for information brokerage, designed as part of the ACTS project GAIA, Generic Architecture for Information Availability. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes a go-between service that helps people find information from many providers, like a librarian who knows many libraries.

questions: what is a functional unit manager
subtitle: A generic architecture for brokering information between customers and suppliers in electronic markets.

tldr.problem: In electronic markets, customers struggle to find products and suppliers because of the huge number of offerings and the heterogeneity of existing protocols and formats. Customers and suppliers cannot manage the complexity alone.
tldr.mechanism: GAIA defines a broker-based architecture where a broker intermediates between customers and suppliers. The broker hides complexity and heterogeneity through a modular design with technology-independent functional units (FUMs) that coordinate with technology-dependent functional units (FUs). Four core actions—Search, Locate, Order, and Deliver—are supported by a kernel and supporting helpers for authentication and payment.
tldr.outcome: This provides a flexible framework for e-commerce systems where new technologies can be plugged in without disrupting the overall brokerage system, and customers interact with a single broker rather than managing relationships with many suppliers.

today: RFC 2552 is an Informational RFC describing the GAIA architecture from the EU ACTS research project. While the research project concluded, the concepts remain relevant for understanding broker-based e-commerce systems and modular information architecture design.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Today's electronic markets have an overwhelming number of suppliers and products. Customers cannot efficiently search for what they want or locate it, and the protocols and formats used by different suppliers are all different. This heterogeneity makes it impossible for a single customer system to handle all the variations.

GAIA (Generic Architecture for Information Availability) is a research project funded by the EU ACTS programme. It defines a domain-independent and supplier-independent architecture for information brokerage. A broker acts as an intermediary, hiding the complexity and heterogeneity of the supply chain from the customer. The customer system provides only a unified user interface; the broker handles all the protocol conversions and interactions with multiple suppliers.

The brokerage system allows customers to search for products, locate suppliers, order products, and receive delivery—all through the broker, without needing to manage direct relationships with individual suppliers.
sections.plainLanguage: When there are too many shops and too many different ways they do business, a broker steps in as a middleman. You tell the broker what you want, and it finds it from any supplier, orders it, and delivers it to you in a simple, uniform way.

sections.title: The GAIA Reference Model and Roles
sections.content:
GAIA defines three principal roles in a transaction: Customer, Broker, and Supplier. The customer initiates the transaction by requesting actions and receives results. The broker responds to customer requests and may in turn request services from other brokers or suppliers. The supplier is the source of products and provides information about them to the broker.

Supporting these three roles are Helpers—auxiliary entities that provide services like authentication (verifying identity), payment (handling financial transactions), and security (encryption, signatures). These helpers participate in GAIA transactions but are outside the core trading logic.

A GAIA transaction comprises four core Actions: Search (find products matching a description), Locate (find suppliers and availability information), Order (negotiate terms and commit to purchase), and Deliver (receive the product). These actions may occur in sequence or independently depending on the customer's needs and the nature of the product.
sections.plainLanguage: In a GAIA transaction, you are the customer asking for something. The broker finds it, talks to suppliers about it, and arranges payment. Helpers like payment services and security services support these main roles.

sections.title: Broker Architecture: Kernel, Managers, and Units
sections.content:
The GAIA brokerage system is built in three layers. At the bottom are Functional Units (FUs)—technology-dependent adapters that know how to talk to specific protocols (e.g., Z39.50 for searching, FTP for delivery). Each FU translates abstract operations from the broker into protocol-specific commands.

Above the FUs are Functional Unit Managers (FUMs)—technology-independent orchestrators. There is one FUM for each major function: Search FUM, Locate FUM, Order FUM, Customer FUM, Delivery FUM, Authentication FUM, and Payment FUM. Each FUM accepts abstract primitive operations from the broker kernel and routes them to the appropriate FU based on what the situation requires (e.g., choosing which search protocol to use). This modular design allows new FUs and technologies to be plugged in without changing the rest of the broker.

At the top is the Kernel, which acts as a message bus. It coordinates the FUMs, synchronizes the sequence of actions within a transaction, and maintains the context that flows from one action to the next. When a customer initiates a search, the kernel invokes the Search FUM, which selects the appropriate search FU, and so on through the transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: The broker has three levels: the kernel at the top makes decisions and schedules work, managers in the middle pick which technology to use, and units at the bottom actually talk to suppliers using their languages.

sections.title: Search, Locate, Order, and Deliver
sections.content:
Search: The customer describes a desired product to the broker, which searches on the customer's behalf and returns a list of matching products by identifier. The broker may consult multiple suppliers and aggregate results.

Locate: Given a product identifier, the customer asks the broker to find available sources. The broker returns information about suppliers and availability terms (delivery methods, time, cost). These terms are provisional and may be negotiated in the Order action.

Order: The customer asks the broker or supplier to obtain a product. The order action includes a negotiation phase where the customer receives a quotation with final terms, and a purchase phase where the customer commits. If supported, the broker may facilitate synchronous negotiation (e.g., via telepresence) for complex deals.

Deliver: The broker or supplier provides the product to the customer. Products may be information, physical objects, or metadata. Delivery can occur in response to an order, or independently as follow-up to a search or locate action.

These actions are coordinated by the kernel and carried out through the appropriate FUMs and FUs, which handle the protocol-specific details transparently to the customer.
sections.plainLanguage: The broker does four things in order: search for what the customer wants, find out where to get it, negotiate and purchase it, then deliver it. Each step uses the right technology for the supplier involved.

sections.title: Helpers and Supporting Architecture
sections.content:
Beyond the four core trading actions, GAIA transactions may involve Helpers. Authentication Helpers verify the identity of actors to each other during any action. Payment Helpers manage financial transfers. Security Helpers provide encryption, digital signatures, and data integrity verification. The manner and method of each helper service is left to implementations; GAIA defines when they may be invoked but not how.

The GAIA Standard Profiles define mandatory and optional conformance levels. Some brokers may implement only Search and Locate actions, others only Delivery, and others the full set. This modular approach allows implementations to start simple and add capabilities incrementally. The technology-independent nature of FUMs and the pluggable nature of FUs ensure that as new protocols and technologies emerge, they can be integrated into a GAIA broker without redesigning the core.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers are extra services like checking who you are, taking your payment, or scrambling data so it is secret. The main broker does not need to know how they work—it just asks for help when needed.
